newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel considers further peace steps.
newsitem.headline: Israel considers further peace steps.

text.p: Israel's cabinet met on Monday to discuss further troop pullouts from the West Bank, ahead of a U.S. visit by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later this week.

Netanyahu is to hold talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday. The cabinet session followed a summit late on Sunday between Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on the future of the Israeli-PLO peace process.

The Monday meeting centred on presentations by senior military planning and legal officials, who discussed a timetable for future withdrawals, division of military responsibilities, and other issues, the cabinet secretary said in a statement.
"The cabinet will discuss further questions of the redeployment toward the end of the month," he said. No decisions were taken at the Monday meeting, officials said.

An Israel-PLO deal on Hebron set March 7 as the start of a three-stage troop withdrawal from rural areas still under Israeli occupation in the West Bank. The pullbacks are to be completed by mid-1998.

In a peace breakthrough in January, Israel handed 80 percent of the West Bank town of Hebron to PLO rule, ending months of rancorous debate both with the Palestinians and within Netanyahu's right-wing cabinet.
Arafat arrived in Hebron on Monday to spend the last day of the Moslem feast of Eid al-Fitr in the West Bank.

His two-day visit could coincide with the release by Israel of 25 Palestinian women prisoners. Asked when the women would be freed, Arafat told Reuters after his arrival he expected "very good news within the next few hours". He did not elaborate.
An Israeli security source said the prisoners would be freed on Tuesday to the West Bank town of Ramallah.

Foreign Minister David Levy told army radio on Monday the cabinet faced a decision on whether the withdrawal would be made in areas currently under joint Israeli-PLO control, or if territory now under exclusive Israeli authority would also be handed over to Palestinian self-rule.

Prior to the Hebron pullout -- agreed with Israel's previous Labour government but suspended after Islamic suicide bombings early last year -- Arabs had voiced fears that the hawkish Netanyahu, elected last May, might bring peace moves to a halt.
Netanyahu said on Sunday he and Arafat had agreed to start detailed talks on future steps outlined in the Hebron pact.
"We agreed on a mechanism to resolve these issues and advance them," he said. Israeli-PLO teams will begin talks next Sunday, with a economics panel meeting before that.

Levy said the cabinet would decide on the additional pullout solely on the basis of security considerations. He reiterated Israel's insistence that it alone will determine the nature and depth of the pullbacks. The PLO insists they must be negotiated.

Arafat has complained of delays on other issues in the Hebron deal, including the operation of Palestinian sea and air ports, the release of Palestinian prisoners and "free passage" between Gaza and the West Bank.

"A month after the Hebron protocol was signed, many things should have been implemented, including the release of women (prisoners), but until now nothing has been implemented," Arafat's aide Nabil Abu Rdeinah told Reuters on Monday.
U.S. officials have expressed hopes that agreement on Hebron could pave the way for resumption of talks with Syria.
The Syrian track, seen as the cornerstone to an overall Middle East peace deal, has long been stalled over the strategic Golan Heights, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.
Netanyahu's office said the prime minister met Golan settlers on Monday to hear their views before his U.S. trip.
